title: Using AI to help formulate a trading strategy using fundamental data
author: Sure-Function7604
selftext:
I wanted to see if Claude could help me create a trading strategy using some commercial software. My goal wasn’t to see if AI could make me a winning strategy, it was to see if it could help me create a process for creating investment strategies. Those are similar, but different things.



I told Claude I was interested in creating a stock investing strategy that had a similar risk-adjusted return to the S&P 500, but with lower volatility (lower beta). I told it to treat me like a beginner and to walk me through the process step-by-step.

  
For context, the software uses fundamental company data (things like profit margins, debt to equity, revenue growth rates, etc.) instead of technical indicators.



Claude started out by reading the software documentation and formulated a plan to test the strategy. One thing that impressed me is that Claude recommended training the strategy on data from 2016-2024 for two reasons: the data was not survivorship bias free pre-2026, and it wanted to hold out the last 2 years so I didn't test the strategy on data it was trained on.



The part that did not impress me is that it came in with a preferred set of metrics before I even shared any data with it. Before I even opened the software, it had already picked a handful of metrics to use for the strategy. So it clearly had some bias. However, Claude walked me through using the software to do some statistical tests on the metrics (calculating information coefficients). After it saw those results it decided to drop some of the metrics that it assumed would work because their information coefficient was too low. So it at least recognized that, but it still seemed weird that it came up with metrics before looking at any data.



I finished creating the strategy using Claude's recommendations and tested it from 2024-2026. On the two unseen years it came in close to the index on risk-adjusted return, with a lower raw return and a noticeably smaller worst drawdown. So it came close to the goals I gave it, a similar risk-adjusted return with lower volatility, but it landed just under the index on Sharpe. To be fair, the S&P 500 had a 20% annualized return in the timeframe tested, which is difficult to beat.



Overall, I think using AI in a way like this was useful to get started and learn the software, but still requires some human intervention. If I were to do it again, I would challenge it more and ask it to analyze the data from the software in more detail, and explain to me in detail why it chose the metrics it chose.

  
Has anyone else used AI as a learning tool like this?

  
Full disclosure: I am the creator of the software, and did this test because I thought it would be a fun way to test AI and double as a tutorial for new users to the software. I recorded the full thing for YouTube, and wrote an article on Substack about it. The point of this post is to share the idea of using AI to help create a process, not promote my software. If you're interested in reading more in depth about the test, you can read it at: [https://quantascent.substack.com/p/i-had-claude-design-a-stock-strategy](https://quantascent.substack.com/p/i-had-claude-design-a-stock-strategy)

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: holding out later years is good. with fundamentals the trap that bites next is reporting dates: if the software stamps a quarter's numbers at quarter end instead of the day they were filed, the backtest knows earnings about six weeks early, and low-beta screens look great on that.

replies.author: Sure-Function7604
replies.body: That is a very good point. The fundamentals use the filing date, but the "key-metrics" and "ratios" that I get from the data provider (P/E, ROIC, etc.) don't come stamped with the filing date. For those, I get them at quarter end + 45 days. But now you have me worrying that might not be the best way to handle that. I'm gonna comb through the data and make sure that fallback is actually appropriate. There's probably a better way to handle that. Thanks for flagging that!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: quarter end + 45 is fine for most 10-Qs, but 10-Ks get 60-90 days and late filers blow past that, so I'd compute the ratios myself from filing-date fundamentals. that blind-to-the-future check was the first thing I put into Quantradin when I built it. quantradin.com

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: good luck with it. spot check one ticker's filing dates by hand before trusting the whole run.

comments.author: Kun-Armando
comments.body: Nice write-up, and thanks for being upfront about being the creator. One thing that stood out: the S&P did 20% annualized in your test window, which is a tough bar for a low-beta strategy. Have you tried it over a stretch where the market fell? That’s where it would show whether it does what it promises.

replies.author: Sure-Function7604
replies.body: Love that idea! I have been testing different time frames and different strategies for a few years now. But I haven't done a "methodical test" where I plan things out and document everything for that yet. I'll add that to the todo list because the fundamental thing I'm trying to answer right now is: "does scoring stocks on their fundamental data actually give you an edge?" Because the market is insanely efficient and difficult (if not impossible) to predict, so quantifying things that can be learned from the data is important to me, even if it's not "do these things and get better returns"
